author: ohtadmin
title: Trio of artists will be exhibited at library
text:
Three artists sharing water zodiac signs are aptly being displayed together in a building that is within a half-mile walk from the ocean on both its eastern and western sides.
The Jamestown Philomenian Library is exhibiting Rick Meli, Ernie Wulff and Jane Kaminski through Nov. 28. The different mediums and styles, ranging from realistic photography to abstract painting, are united as all three artists have work depicting water on display.
“He’s a Scorpio, Jane and I are both Pisces,” Wulff said. “All water signs. It sounds corny, but it is kind of cute.”
Meli said the idea for the show came from a fortuitous circumstance. He originally asked curator Jillian Barber to be featured in the monthly display, and at the same time, his friend, Wulff, both of Jamestown, also was inquiring about an open space in the calendar. Barber suggested they do it together.
“We talked about doing a show together for a number of years,” Meli said, “and it finally came together.”
Kaminski, of Narragansett, came into the fold when she displayed her work alongside Meli and Wulff during the open-studios tour organized in August by the Jamestown Arts Center. She showed the men her portfolio.
“We liked her work,” Meli said. “We thought it fit with ours, like an in-between. His work, her work and then my work.”
Barber said this exhibition is the first three-artist show she can remember in her 28 years organizing the displays.
Meli last displayed his seascapes at the library in 2020. He creates his paintings using a variety of media, including acrylic paint, pastel, pen and watercolor. Meli is a retired art historian and former University of Rhode Island instructor who has always been drawn to nature scenes.
“Most of my life, I have made art that is of nature,” he said. “Seascapes have been an interest to me for a number of years, especially when I moved here to Jamestown. Being close to the ocean, I spend a lot of time near the ocean. Seascapes seem to be a natural evolution.”
Altogether, Meli has eight pieces on display all painted in the last year, including one that was finished about a month ago. Among the paintings in the show is “Beavertail Break,” a pastel piece that Meli painted about six months ago, which depicts a wave crashing into a rock near Beavertail State Park.
“After one of the storms we had, and there was a lot of heavy surf, it had cleared up, but there was a lot of turbulence and heavy sea,” Meli said. “I made a few sketches, took a few pictures and then I worked on it.”
“Full Moon Swells,” a night scene of waves crashing over rocks, is Meli’s favorite of his paintings in the show. He said the piece is “very dramatic.”
Wulff works in oil and acrylic painting and also has been a film photographer for 55 years. He chose his work in the show based on the color.
“This time of year, color is so important,” he said. “I’m very much a color person. Color invokes happiness. I love color; color has a good meaning to it.”
Wulff’s section of the show features a depiction of Zeek’s Creek with a heron in the middle, alongside abstract works and a photograph of the Newport Pell Bridge at night. Wulff said he took that photo on Christmas Eve during a full moon. The photo is titled “Green Cross,” both because there is a green cross in the middle, and the play on words of it depicting traffic across the green-colored bridge.
As a curator, Wulff said he appreciates all art, and the different styles that are featured in the show. He is also glad that Barber has continued to curate local art at the library.
“She has given me a privilege,” he said. “She loves the arts, and she’s a very talented human being.”
Kaminski said she had been dormant as a painter for about 15 years, and Wulff has been encouraging her to pick her pencils and brushes back up. Her piece in the show depicting a monarch butterfly was her first attempt at using acrylic paint, and her work in the show also includes other mediums and styles.
“I did want to show some diversity, but at the same time, I want to push myself to try something different, and not play it so safe,” she said. “When I looked at everything together, it’s a little puzzle of me.”
Kaminski has four pieces in the show, including a large photograph of the Beavertail Lighthouse, which Meli and Wulff requested be included as thematically appropriate for a Jamestown show.
The photograph was taken six years ago, and she spent about 90 minutes waiting for the light to turn so she could finally snap a picture. Kaminski said she thinks the photograph complements Meli’s Beavertail seascapes because they are different interpretations of the same spot. Another of Kaminski’s pieces is a sketch of a feather she collected while walking along a beach.
“I think there’s something about the simple beauty in it,” Kaminski said.
Kaminski said she hopes visitors to the library see how she, Meli and Wulff express themselves in different ways. Meli said he heard from staff that children have been positively commenting on the colors and textures.
“A lot of children have been stopping and looking at it,” Meli said.
